new_statements.quote: On the analysis we present here, Golin is a word-tone language with three contrasting tones – high, mid and low – associated at the level of the word (or perhaps the foot). Tones are attached to the rightmost mora of their domain, with a relatively constant pitch realization at that point, but more freedom in the rest of the domain, giving rise to considerable variation at the etic level of pitch contours over the word. [p. 3] ... The phonological contrast involves several tonal patterns (namely three), rather than just location as in a pitch-accent language. And by possessing several distinct tonal patterns, associated to a domain larger than the syllable, it is clearly a word- or foot-tone rather than a syllable-tone language. [p. 26]

This source supplies the prosodic type: a three-tone word-tone language, no word stress posited, tone anchored on the rightmost mora. Nothing to contradict; it fills the empty entry. new_statements.rule_in_words: Golin (Chris Kia Aina's variety) is a word-tone (or foot-tone) language with a three-way H/M/L contrast whose tone attaches to the rightmost mora of the word; the word-level prosodic contrast is a tonal pattern, not a location contrast, and the chapter posits no word stress at all. The only mentions of 'stress' are in Hayata's typology table (Russian, English as stress languages, p. 26) and in two footnotes by Lee (p. 35 fn. 8: vowel back-shift 'might depend, for instance, on prominence (e.g. stress, even tone?)'; p. 49 fn. 26), which leave prominence unanalysed.
new_statements.exceptions: The analysis is explicitly restricted to Kia's dialect and to nominal words (verbs excluded, p. 9, p. 7); the Bunns' earlier two-tone syllable-tone analysis (Bunn & Bunn 1970, Bunn 1974) is rejected for Kia's variety but the authors note the Bunns' variety has a different 'tune' and 'we cannot be certain whether the variety described by the Bunns would yield to reanalysis' (pp. 7, 26). Donohue (1997) listed Golin as a syllable-tone language on the Bunns' data; Evans & Stoakes say this is 'clearly not to be the case for Kia's variety' (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: Evans & Stoakes 2005 describe the Golin of a single speaker, Chris Kia Aina ('Kia's dialect', p. 9), and restrict the tonal analysis to nominal words; they contrast it with the variety described by Gordon and Ruth Bunn (SIL, 1970/1974), which Kia said has a different 'tune'. Dom, described by Tida (2000, 2003) as a word-tone language, is noted as mutually comprehensible with Golin (p. 8).

audit.recode_to: no reclassification. Keep classification weight (tone-driven), edge='unbounded' (stress on rightmost H-toned syllable, else final syllable; compounds stress first H, note 7). Add to contra/caution: Evans & Stoakes 2005 (Materials on Golin pp.3-29) reanalyse a neighbouring sub-variety (speaker Chris Kia Aina) as three-way word tone (H/M/L) with the tone-defining pitch target on the last mora of the domain, reject the Bunns' two-way syllable-tone premise for that variety, and posit no word stress; they call the account preliminary and state (p.26) they 'cannot be certain whether the variety described by the Bunns would yield to reanalysis'.
